listeningParts.title: Enrolling in a robotics holiday club
listeningParts.contextDescription: A mother phones a children's robotics club to book a summer course for her son.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Kingsley Robotics Club, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I'm ringing about your summer holiday courses. My son is absolutely obsessed with building things at the moment, and a friend of mine said her daughter went to one of your courses last year and loved it.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's great to hear. We run two courses for children over the summer, depending on their age. Can I ask how old your son is?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He's eleven. He'll be twelve in October.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Right. So our Junior Builders course is for seven- to nine-year-olds, and that's mostly about building simple moving models with motors and gears. For his age, the better option would be Code Explorers, which is for ten- to thirteen-year-olds. On that course, children build a small wheeled robot from a kit and then learn to program it so that it can follow a line, avoid obstacles and respond to sounds.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That sounds perfect. He's done a bit of coding at school, but nothing with real machines. Does he need any experience?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Not at all. Most children are complete beginners. The instructors are university engineering students, and they're very good at explaining things step by step. We also keep the groups small, with no more than eight children per instructor.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Good. And when do the courses run?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Each course lasts one week, Monday to Friday. Code Explorers runs four times over the summer. I'm afraid the week beginning the twenty-eighth of July is already full, but we still have places in the week beginning the fourth of August, and in the last two weeks of August.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: We're away at the end of August, so the fourth of August would be best.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. Now, I should mention that during the summer we don't use our usual building in Kingsley, because it's being repainted. The courses will be held at Ashford Primary School, on Mill Lane. We'll be using the school library, which has plenty of space and good internet access.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I know Ashford, it's not far from us. What about the cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The full price for the week is one hundred and seventy-five pounds. If you were a member of the club, it would be one hundred and fifty, but membership is only for children who come to our weekly Saturday sessions during term time. To hold the place, we ask for a deposit of thirty pounds, and the rest is due two weeks before the course starts.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Fine. Does that include the robot kit?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, all the equipment is included, and at the end of the week each child takes their robot home, so they can carry on programming it. Children just need to bring a packed lunch and a drink. Oh, and on Wednesday afternoon we go outside to the school field to fly small drones, so they should bring a sun hat, in case it's hot.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He'll love the drones. What time does it start and finish?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Doors open at a quarter to nine, and sessions start at nine. From Monday to Thursday, pick-up is at quarter past four. On Friday, we finish a little earlier, at half past three, because there's a final competition, and parents are invited to come and watch the robots race around an obstacle course.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, that'll be fun. I'll try to get the afternoon off work.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Now, could I take some details? What's your son's name?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It's Toby Westacott. That's W-E-S-T-A-C-O-T-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And is there anything we should know about his health?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: He has asthma, but it's mild. He carries an inhaler with him, and he knows how to use it.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's fine, I'll add a note to his form, and the instructors are all trained in first aid. Could I have a phone number for you, in case we need to contact you during the day?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll email you a link so you can pay the deposit online, and a consent form for photographs. We sometimes put pictures of the robots on our website, but only with permission.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That's fine. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A new exhibition about robots
listeningParts.contextDescription: A museum curator introduces a new exhibition about robots and artificial intelligence to a group of visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to the Northgate Science Museum. My name is Rachel Dumont, and I'm the curator of our new exhibition, Machines Like Us, which opened just last week. Before you go in, I'd like to give you a quick overview, so you can plan your visit and make sure you don't miss anything.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The exhibition took nearly three years to put together. Originally, we planned a small display about the history of factory robots, but as we started talking to researchers, we realised that what visitors really wanted to know was how robots and artificial intelligence are going to affect their everyday lives. So the focus changed, and the exhibition became much bigger. It now fills the whole of the second floor.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The first thing I'd like to stress is that this isn't an exhibition where you just look at objects behind glass. Most of the robots here are working machines, and many of them are interactive. You'll be able to talk to them, play games with them and, in some cases, teach them to do simple tasks. Because of that, some of the displays can get very busy, especially at weekends, so I'd recommend visiting the most popular galleries first.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Let me take you through the galleries in order. The first gallery is called Ancestors. It looks at the long history of machines that imitate living things, from clockwork figures made in the eighteenth century to the first industrial robots of the 1960s. The star object here is a beautiful mechanical writer, a doll that can write short messages with a real pen. It's very delicate, so it's only switched on twice a day, at eleven and at three. If you want to see it move, make sure you're there at the right time.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The second gallery is The Factory Floor. Here you'll find a full-sized robot arm of the kind used in car factories. It's been programmed to sort coloured blocks, and you can challenge it to a race to see who's faster. I should warn you that almost nobody wins. For safety reasons, the arm is behind a transparent screen, and children under eight must be accompanied by an adult in this area.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Next comes the gallery called At Home. This one is about robots that people actually live with, such as robot vacuum cleaners and lawnmowers. What's interesting here is that it shows how often these machines fail. There's a fun section where you can watch videos of robots getting stuck under sofas or falling down stairs. It's a reminder that homes are much more difficult environments for robots than factories, because everything is constantly being moved around.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The fourth gallery, Caring Machines, looks at robots in hospitals and care homes. There's a robotic seal that's used to comfort elderly patients, and you're welcome to stroke it. We've also got a surgical robot, although it's not working, I'm afraid; it's a prototype that was donated by a hospital. Next to it, there's a short film in which surgeons explain how they control these machines from a console a few metres away from the patient.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The fifth gallery is called Thinking Machines, and it's about artificial intelligence. Rather than robots, it's mostly screens. You can play a game against a computer that learns from your moves, and try to tell the difference between poems written by people and poems written by software. Many visitors find that harder than they expect.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: The final gallery, Tomorrow, is a little different. It doesn't have many objects. Instead, it asks you questions about the future, for example whether you'd trust a robot to look after a child, and you vote using a touch screen. The results are displayed on a large wall, so you can compare your answers with everyone else's. We're collecting these votes for a research project with the local university.

dialogue.speaker: Curator
dialogue.text: Just a couple of practical points before you go in. Photography is allowed everywhere except in Caring Machines, because the film there includes real patients. The café on the ground floor is open until four, and there's a shop next to the exit where you can buy simple robot kits. Okay, enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: A project on robots in elderly care
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two social care students, Megan and Josh, discuss their research project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Megan, Josh. Come and sit down. So you wanted to talk about your project on robots in elderly care. How far have you got?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, we've done most of the reading, and last week we visited a care home that's been trying out a social robot for six months. We've got a lot of notes, but we're not sure how to organise the report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Let's start with the reading, then. What did you find?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The most researched robot by far is PARO, the robotic seal that was developed in Japan. It responds to touch and to voices, and it moves its head and makes sounds a bit like a baby seal. There are quite a few studies of it being used with people with dementia.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what do those studies show?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Some of them found that residents were calmer and less anxious after sessions with the robot, and that they talked to each other more. But a lot of the studies were quite small, and some were funded by people connected with the company, so we decided we couldn't rely on them too much.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a very sensible thing to notice. Make sure you say that in your literature review. What about the visit?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: That was really interesting. The home we went to is using a different kind of robot. It's about the size of a small child, it has a screen for a face, and it leads activities like quizzes, music sessions and gentle exercises. The manager told us they introduced it because they'd had problems recruiting enough staff, not to replace anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: And what surprised me was that the residents were much more positive about it than I'd expected. I thought older people might be suspicious of technology, but most of the ones we spoke to just found it fun. One woman said it was the only thing in the home that never got tired of her stories.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a lovely quotation. Did you get permission to use it?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Yes, everyone we interviewed signed a consent form, and we're not using any real names.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And what did the staff think?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Their views were more mixed. The activities coordinator liked it, because it meant she could spend more time with residents who needed one-to-one attention. But two of the care assistants were worried that the management might eventually use robots as an excuse to cut staff. And one nurse said that when the robot broke down for a week, some residents were quite upset, which made her wonder whether they were becoming too attached to it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a really important ethical question. In fact, I'd suggest you make ethics a separate section of the report, rather than mixing it in with the findings. Issues like attachment, privacy and whether it's honest to give someone with dementia a robot animal deserve proper discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Privacy came up too. The robot has a camera, and some families didn't like the idea that it might be recording their relatives.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Did the home say what happens to the recordings?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The manager said the camera is only used to recognise faces, and nothing is stored. But she admitted that most families had never asked.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. Now, for the structure. You could start with a short introduction explaining why this matters, for example the growing number of older people and the shortage of care workers in many countries. Then the literature review, then your method, then the findings from the visit, and then the ethics section. Finish with recommendations.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: How long should it be?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: The limit is four thousand words. Don't go over it, because you'll lose marks. And I'd like to see a draft of the literature review by Friday the fourteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We were also thinking of including some photographs of the robot.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as no residents appear in them. Actually, a simple table comparing the different types of care robot would be more useful than photos. Put it in the appendix.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Great, thanks. That's really helpful.

listeningParts.title: The early history of artificial intelligence
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a computer science course on how the field of artificial intelligence developed in the twentieth century.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to step back from the technical material and look at the history of artificial intelligence. It's a history full of big promises, bitter disappointments and surprising comebacks, and knowing it will help you judge some of the claims you hear about AI today.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: A good place to start is 1950, when the British mathematician Alan Turing published a paper called 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. Turing thought that the question 'Can machines think?' was too vague to answer, so he replaced it with a test, which he called the imitation game. A human judge has a written conversation with two hidden partners, one a person and one a machine. If the judge can't reliably tell which is which, Turing argued, we have no good reason to deny that the machine is intelligent. We now call this the Turing test, and it's still discussed, although most researchers no longer think it's a useful goal.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The field got its name a few years later. In 1955, the computer scientist John McCarthy and three colleagues wrote a proposal for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States, and in it they used the phrase 'artificial intelligence'. The workshop took place in 1956, and it's usually seen as the birth of AI as a research field. The organisers were extremely optimistic. They believed that significant progress could be made on problems such as language and learning in a single summer.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For the next twenty years or so, most AI research was what we call symbolic. The idea was that intelligence consisted of manipulating symbols according to rules, so if you could write down the right rules, a computer could reason like a person. And there were some impressive early results. Programs were written that could prove mathematical theorems and play draughts. In the mid-1960s, Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT created a program called ELIZA, which imitated a therapist by turning the user's statements into questions. It was very simple, but some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed Weizenbaum.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, the early optimism didn't last. Problems that seemed easy, like understanding ordinary language or recognising objects, turned out to be extremely hard, and computers at the time were very slow and had tiny memories. In Britain, a government report written by the mathematician James Lighthill in 1973 concluded that AI had failed to achieve its grand aims, and funding was cut sharply. Similar cuts happened in the United States. This period of reduced funding and interest became known as the first AI winter.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the 1980s, interest returned, thanks largely to expert systems. These were programs that tried to capture the knowledge of human specialists, such as doctors or engineers, in the form of thousands of if-then rules. Some were commercially successful, but they were expensive to build and to update, and they were brittle: if they met a situation the rules didn't cover, they failed completely. By the late 1980s, the market had collapsed, and a second winter followed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, a different approach had been developing quietly. Instead of writing rules, researchers built neural networks, which are loosely inspired by the brain, and which learn patterns from examples. Frank Rosenblatt had built an early version, the perceptron, in the late 1950s, but for decades these networks were limited by a lack of data and computing power.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Two famous events showed how much things had changed. In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue computer defeated the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a six-game match. Deep Blue mostly relied on enormous speed, examining millions of positions per second. Then, in 2012, a neural network won an image recognition competition by a huge margin, using powerful graphics processors originally designed for video games. That result convinced many researchers to switch to the approach now called deep learning. And in 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo program beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's best players of the board game Go, which had been considered far harder for computers than chess.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what's the lesson? Progress in AI hasn't been steady. It's come in waves, driven as much by data and hardware as by new ideas. Next week, we'll look at how modern language models work.

readingPassages.title: The chess-playing machine that fooled Europe
paragraphs: In 1770, at the imperial palace of Schönbrunn in Vienna, a civil servant named Wolfgang von Kempelen presented a remarkable invention to the Empress Maria Theresa and her court. It consisted of a large wooden cabinet, on top of which sat a life-sized figure of a man dressed in robes and a turban, holding a long pipe in one hand. Kempelen announced that this figure, which soon became known as the Turk, could play chess against any human opponent. To the astonishment of the audience, it did exactly that, moving the pieces with its mechanical arm and usually winning.

Kempelen took great care to persuade spectators that the machine was genuine. Before each game, he opened the doors of the cabinet one by one and held a candle behind them, so that the audience could see an elaborate collection of gears, wheels and levers inside. He then closed the doors, wound up the machine with a key and invited a volunteer to play. During the game, the figure would nod its head when it threatened its opponent's queen, and if a player attempted an illegal move, it would shake its head and move the piece back to its original square.

In reality, the Turk was an ingenious illusion. Hidden inside the cabinet was a skilled human chess player, who could slide from one section to another on a moving seat while the doors were being opened, so that he was never seen. The operator followed the game by watching small metal discs beneath the board, which were pulled upwards by magnets in the chess pieces above. He then controlled the figure's arm using a system of levers, and worked by the light of a candle. The machinery that the audience saw was largely there to distract them.

Curiously, Kempelen himself does not seem to have been particularly proud of the Turk. He regarded it as a clever entertainment rather than a serious achievement, and for long periods he refused to exhibit it, preferring to work on other projects, including a machine that could imitate human speech. However, in the early 1780s, he was persuaded to take the Turk on a tour of Europe, and it attracted large crowds in cities such as Paris and London. Wherever it went, writers and scientists published articles attempting to explain how it worked, although few came close to the truth.

After Kempelen's death in 1804, the Turk was bought by Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, a Bavarian musician and showman who is also remembered for producing and promoting the metronome. Maelzel made the act more theatrical and took the machine on further tours. In 1809, according to a famous account, the Turk played against Napoleon Bonaparte, who had occupied Vienna, and easily defeated him. Among the many people who saw the Turk in action was the English mathematician Charles Babbage, who later designed some of the earliest mechanical computers and who was fascinated by the question of whether a machine could really play chess.

In 1826, Maelzel took the Turk across the Atlantic to the United States, where it toured for more than a decade. There, it inspired one of the best-known attempts to expose it: an essay published in 1836 by the writer Edgar Allan Poe. Poe argued correctly that a human player must be hidden inside, partly because the machine did not always win, which he believed a true machine would. Some of his other reasoning, however, was mistaken.

After Maelzel died in 1838, the Turk passed through several owners and eventually ended up in a museum in Philadelphia. In 1854, a fire swept through the building and destroyed it. A few years later, the son of its last owner published a series of articles that finally revealed exactly how the illusion had been performed, ending more than eighty years of speculation.

Although the Turk was a fraud, its influence was real. It encouraged people to ask whether thinking could be mechanised, a question that would later become central to computer science. In the twentieth century, chess became a standard test for artificial intelligence, and in 1997 a real machine, IBM's Deep Blue, defeated the world champion. Even the Turk's name lives on: in 2005, the company Amazon launched a service called Mechanical Turk, through which businesses pay people to carry out small tasks, such as labelling images, that computers still find difficult. The name is an honest joke, since, like the original, the service relies on human intelligence hidden behind a machine.

readingPassages.title: Why robots struggle with the easy things
paragraphs: In 1961, a machine called Unimate began work at a General Motors car factory in New Jersey. It was a heavy hydraulic arm that lifted hot pieces of metal from a casting machine and stacked them, a dangerous job that had injured many workers. Unimate is generally regarded as the first industrial robot, and it was the product of a partnership between the inventor George Devol, who had patented the idea, and the engineer Joseph Engelberger, who turned it into a business. Within two decades, robot arms were welding, painting and assembling cars in factories across the world.

Today, the most automated economies have astonishing numbers of these machines. According to the International Federation of Robotics, South Korea has around one thousand industrial robots for every ten thousand manufacturing workers, and countries such as Singapore, China, Germany and Japan also have very high densities. Yet if you visit almost any factory, you will notice that robots are concentrated in certain kinds of work. They weld and paint with superhuman precision, but many apparently simple tasks, such as folding a towel, sorting a pile of mixed objects or plugging in a flexible cable, are still done by people.

Researchers noticed this puzzle decades ago. In the 1980s, scientists including Hans Moravec, Rodney Brooks and Marvin Minsky pointed out that the tasks people find difficult, such as playing chess or solving equations, are often relatively easy for computers, while those that even a small child performs without thinking, such as recognising a face or walking across a crowded room, are extremely hard. Moravec wrote in 1988 that it was comparatively easy to make computers perform like adults on intelligence tests, but very difficult to give them the perception and mobility of a one-year-old. This observation is now known as Moravec's paradox.

Moravec offered an evolutionary explanation. Skills such as seeing, grasping and moving have been refined by natural selection over hundreds of millions of years, and the brain devotes enormous resources to them. Because they are so well practised, we perform them unconsciously and therefore underestimate how complex they are. Abstract reasoning, by contrast, is a recent development in evolutionary terms. It feels difficult to us precisely because we are not very good at it, and it can often be reduced to a small number of clear rules that a computer can follow.

A related idea comes from the philosopher Michael Polanyi, who wrote in 1966 that 'we can know more than we can tell'. A person can ride a bicycle or recognise a friend's voice without being able to explain how. This kind of tacit knowledge creates a problem for engineers, because traditional programming requires every step of a task to be specified in advance. If nobody can describe precisely how they tie a shoelace, it is very hard to write instructions that a robot can follow.

The difficulty is especially clear in warehouses. In 2015, the online retailer Amazon organised the first of a series of competitions, the Amazon Picking Challenge, inviting university teams to build robots that could pick individual items from crowded shelves. The items ranged from pencils and books to soft toys and packets of biscuits. The winning robots worked, but they were far slower and less reliable than human workers, struggling in particular with objects that were transparent, shiny, soft or partly hidden behind others.

Recent progress has come from two directions. First, machine learning allows robots to learn from experience rather than relying entirely on rules written by programmers. Instead of being told how to grasp each object, a robot can practise thousands of times, sometimes in computer simulations, and gradually improve. Second, engineers have developed new hardware, including soft grippers made of flexible materials and suction devices, which are more forgiving of small errors than rigid metal fingers. Cheaper cameras and sensors have also helped robots to build a more detailed picture of their surroundings.

Even so, most experts believe that general-purpose robots capable of doing household chores in an ordinary home are still some way off. Homes are unpredictable; objects are constantly moved, lighting changes and every room is different. Factories, on the other hand, can be redesigned around the needs of machines. For the foreseeable future, it seems likely that robots will continue to take over tasks in controlled environments, while the jobs that require ordinary human dexterity, such as cleaning, caring and cooking, will remain surprisingly hard to automate.

readingPassages.title: Will the machines take our jobs?
paragraphs: Fear that machines will make human workers unnecessary is almost as old as industry itself. Between 1811 and 1816, groups of textile workers in the English Midlands and the north of England, who called themselves Luddites after a mythical leader named Ned Ludd, broke into factories at night and smashed the new machines that threatened their livelihoods. Today the word 'Luddite' is used to mock anyone who resists technology, but the original Luddites were not opposed to machines as such. They objected to the way machines were being used to cut wages and replace skilled workers with cheaper, less skilled labour.

In 1930, the economist John Maynard Keynes gave this fear a name. In a short essay entitled 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren', he warned of 'technological unemployment', meaning unemployment caused by our discovering ways of saving labour faster than we can find new uses for it. Yet Keynes was optimistic about the long term. He predicted that within a hundred years, people in wealthy countries would be so productive that they might need to work only around fifteen hours a week, and that the main challenge would be learning how to use their leisure time well.

Keynes was right about productivity, which has risen enormously, but wrong about working hours, which have fallen far less than he expected. And despite two centuries of automation, the long-feared collapse of employment has not occurred. The reason, economists argue, is that technology does not only destroy jobs; it also creates them. When machines make goods cheaper, people spend the money they save on other things, and new industries appear that nobody could have imagined. In 1900, around forty per cent of American workers were employed in agriculture; today the figure is below two per cent, yet unemployment is not remotely forty per cent.

Nevertheless, recent advances in artificial intelligence have revived the old anxiety. In 2013, Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne of the University of Oxford estimated that around forty-seven per cent of jobs in the United States were at high risk of being automated within a decade or two. Their study received enormous publicity. However, other researchers soon pointed out that it assessed entire occupations, whereas most jobs consist of many different tasks, only some of which can be automated. A study for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), published in 2016, took this task-based approach and concluded that only around nine per cent of jobs across OECD countries were at high risk.

A well-known example shows why the task-based view matters. When automated teller machines (ATMs) spread through American banks from the 1970s onwards, many people assumed that bank tellers would disappear. The economist James Bessen found that this did not happen. Because ATMs reduced the cost of running a branch, banks opened many more branches, and the number of tellers remained roughly stable for decades. Their work changed, however: they spent less time counting cash and more time selling financial products and dealing with customers' problems.

This does not mean that automation is harmless. The economist David Autor has shown that, in many wealthy countries, technology has contributed to a 'polarisation' of the labour market. Routine middle-skill jobs, such as clerical and factory work, have declined, while employment has grown in both highly paid professional jobs and in low-paid service work, such as cleaning and care, which is difficult to automate. The result has been rising inequality, as many workers have lost secure, reasonably paid jobs and have been unable to move into better ones.

Will artificial intelligence follow the same pattern? There are reasons to think it may be different. Earlier waves of automation mainly affected physical and routine tasks, but modern AI systems can write, translate, summarise and analyse, which means they may affect educated office workers who previously felt secure. In my view, it would be foolish to assume that, because technology has created more jobs than it destroyed in the past, it will automatically do so again. History is a useful guide, but it is not a guarantee.

At the same time, I believe that the most pessimistic predictions underestimate how much choice societies have. Whether automation leads to shared prosperity or to greater inequality depends heavily on policy: on how education systems prepare people for changing work, on whether workers who lose their jobs are supported while they retrain, and on how the gains from higher productivity are distributed. Technology shapes the possibilities, but it is people who decide which ones become reality. The Luddites lost their battle, but the question they raised, about who benefits from new machines, is as relevant as ever.
